sentences.text: Net income rose from $24.7 billion in FY2016 to $57.0 billion in FY2025, a 9.7% CAGR, while net interest income compounded at 8.4% [F21][F30][F113][F111].
The path was cyclical: net income fell 20.0% in FY2020, rose 65.8% in FY2021 and fell 21.9% in FY2022 [D94][D118][D142].
In FY2023 net interest income rose 33.8% to $89.3 billion [D174][F8], while interest expense rose from $26.1 billion to $81.3 billion [X57][X58].
No firmwide passage gives a cause for that rise, so reading it as a rate-cycle effect is inference, not a reported driver.
Net interest income was 52.3% of FY2025 revenue and grew 3.1% [D209][D221], against 2.4% for noninterest income [D222].
The filing credits the 3.1% NII rise [D221] to higher Markets NII, Card revolving balances and wholesale deposits, partly offset by deposit margin compression and lower rates [P28].
On geographic revenue, EMEA and Asia-Pacific each added 1.2pp to revenue growth [D276][D301], while North America added 0.2pp on 0.3% growth [D251][D250].
Noninterest revenue rose 2.4% [D222] to $87.0 billion [F20]; the absence of the $7.9 billion FY2024 Visa gain predominantly offset the increases [P27].
Diluted EPS rose 1.4% [D216] while proxy-sourced net income fell 2.6% [D214][R1], with the diluted share count down 3.4% [D224].
The efficiency ratio is 52.4% [D207], against a window median of 57.2% [D333], a high of 59.2% [D332] and a low of 51.7% [D331].
Revenue up $4.89 billion [X10][X9], expense up $3.84 billion [X137][X136] and provision up $3.53 billion [X147][X146] took pretax income down 3.3% [X68][X67].
Within Card Services, the filing links a $2.2 billion allowance addition to the Apple Card transaction [P18].
The largest move in the window was in credit cost: the provision fell from 14.6% of revenue in FY2020 [D88] to -7.6% in FY2021 [D112], a 22.2pp swing [D88][D112].
The filing attributes the FY2021 credit benefit, higher net recoveries, to home price improvement and reversals of prior write-downs [P55][D112].
Operating cash flow was -$148 billion in FY2025 [F60] against net income of $57.0 billion [F30], so for a bank it says little about earnings quality.
Buybacks and dividends totalled $48.2 billion [D205], or 84.6% of net income [D205][F30], up from $33.6 billion in FY2024 [D182].
The FY2025 operating outflow reflected higher trading assets, securities borrowed and loans held-for-sale purchases [P21][F60].
Return on average equity was 16.1% [D213], against a seven-bank peer median of 11.8% [D339] and a 100th percentile rank [D338].
Loans were 57.3% of deposits [D211], up 14.2pp from the FY2021 low of 43.1% [D211][D115].
Net loans reached $1.47 trillion [X197] after a $121 billion increase [P4], mainly higher CIB Markets loans and AWM securities-based lending [P4].
Diluted shares fell from 3.65 billion in FY2016 [X83] to 2.78 billion in FY2025 [X92], a 23.8% reduction [X83][X92].
The provision has risen every year since the FY2021 release, reaching $14.2 billion [X147] from $6.39 billion in FY2022 [X144], or 7.8% of revenue [D208].
Together, provision and expense growth absorbed the whole revenue gain, which is the main risk to the earnings path.
Criticized wholesale exposure rose to $48.5 billion from $44.7 billion [P2], though its share fell to 3.4% from 3.5% [P2].
Nonperforming exposure rose $478 million [P3], primarily from downgrades in Technology, Media & Telecommunications, Oil & Gas and Utilities.
The average LCR of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. fell year on year in the fourth quarter, driven by higher lending and dividends to the parent [P10].
A ratio above the 57.2% window median [D333], from 52.4% in FY2025 [D207], would show costs catching up with revenue in the FY2026 10-K.
A provision ratio below 7.8% of revenue [D208] would show the credit rise turning; a rise above it would extend the trend, in the FY2026 10-K.
Criticized wholesale exposure above $48.5 billion [P2] would confirm the downgrade trend, in the FY2026 10-K.
